Cascading retries: A downstream service: Diagnose by correlating request-rate graphs across the call chain - if load on the failing dependency step-changes upward right as its own error rate rises, that is the retry-storm signature (a 'thundering herd' pattern), confirmed by checking retry counters/client logs for exponential growth in attempts per original request. Fix with three layers: exponential backoff with jitter on every retrying client (never fixed-interval retries), a circuit breaker that stops calling a dependency once its error rate crosses a threshold and fails fast instead, and request-level timeouts short enough that failed calls free up resources quickly rather than piling up. Longer-term, add a load-shedding/bulkhead pattern so one degraded dependency cannot exhaust the shared thread/connection pool used by unrelated requests.
Silent data pipeline failure: A daily ET: The root problem is monitoring job success/failure status instead of job output correctness - a job that completes 'successfully' while doing nothing wrong is invisible to naive monitoring. Redesign with data-quality assertions as a pipeline stage: row-count thresholds (alert if today's row count deviates more than a set percentage from a trailing average), null/empty-response detection on the upstream call itself, and schema/freshness checks on the output table (e.g. the latest update timestamp should be within the last 24 hours). Wire these checks to fail the pipeline run itself, not just log a warning, so the failure is loud and blocks anything depending on that data, rather than a passive dashboard people have to remember to look at.
Terraform state conflict: Two engineers: Recover by first running terraform plan to see the exact diff between state and reality without applying anything, using terraform state show/list to inspect suspect resources, and using terraform import or targeted state operations to reconcile state with actual infrastructure rather than blindly re-applying and risking a destructive change. Prevention is a process fix: remote state with locking (a GCS backend with native locking, or Terraform Cloud/Enterprise) so a second apply blocks while one is in progress, and moving to a CI/CD-only apply model with no local applies, so state changes only happen through a single, serialized pipeline with peer-reviewed plan output.
Secrets left in Docker image layers: A s: Explain why this happens - Docker layers are immutable and additive, so a secret written in an earlier layer and later deleted in a subsequent layer still exists in the image's layer history and can be extracted with layer inspection tools. Fix the current image by rotating the leaked credential immediately (assume it is compromised) and rebuilding from a clean Dockerfile using multi-stage builds so secrets used only at build time never enter the final image. Prevent recurrence with build-time secret mounting (BuildKit's --secret flag or an ephemeral build-arg that is never persisted to a layer), pre-commit/CI secret scanning on both source and built images, and treating any credential needed at build time as short-lived and injected only into an ephemeral build stage.
Kubernetes upgrade breaking a webhook: A: Triage live by first checking whether the webhook is configured with failurePolicy: Fail (blocking) - if so, and it is non-critical, temporarily patch it to Ignore or remove the webhook configuration to unblock scheduling immediately, then investigate the actual cause (an API version deprecation between control plane versions, a TLS cert mismatch, or a networking/DNS change affecting the webhook's connectivity). Root-cause with logs from the webhook's pod and by checking the Kubernetes changelog for API removals between the old and new control plane version. Prevent recurrence by testing upgrades against a staging cluster running the same webhooks first, and by defaulting non-critical webhooks to failurePolicy: Ignore combined with strong alerting, so a webhook failure degrades gracefully instead of taking down all pod scheduling.
Cost spike investigation: Cloud spend ju: Start with the cloud billing console's cost breakdown by service/SKU and by day to isolate which service and which day the jump started, then cross-reference with change history (recent deploys, Terraform applies, or autoscaling config changes) around that timestamp. Common root causes to check first: a runaway autoscaler that never scales back down, a misconfigured storage lifecycle policy no longer deleting old data/snapshots, an accidentally public or overly chatty logging/monitoring pipeline generating huge ingestion volume, or a newly introduced retry loop hammering a paid API. Fix the immediate cause, then add budget alerts and per-service cost anomaly detection so the next spike pages someone within hours instead of being found at month-end billing review.
Zombie load balancer backend: A load bal: The mismatch usually means the readiness probe checks something too shallow (e.g. a TCP port check or a health endpoint that always returns 200 regardless of the app's actual ability to serve requests) while the real failure is deeper, such as a dependency the app needs like a database connection pool being exhausted. Fix by making the readiness probe check something meaningful - actually exercise the critical dependency path, or check an internal health flag the app sets when it detects it cannot serve traffic - and pair it with a liveness probe that restarts the pod if it is stuck in a bad state rather than just being marked unready forever. Also verify the load balancer's own health check, if separate from Kubernetes readiness, is configured with the same meaningful check, since a shallow LB-level check can keep sending traffic even if Kubernetes-level readiness is correct.
Multi-tenant noisy neighbor: One team's: Immediate fix: set explicit resource requests/limits and a PriorityClass on the batch job so it is the first thing evicted under pressure, and constrain it to run in its own namespace with a ResourceQuota, ideally on a separate, tainted node pool with a matching toleration only on the batch workload, so it cannot contend for the same nodes as latency-sensitive services at all. Structural fix: schedule the batch job outside business hours if latency is not a hard requirement for it, and adopt namespace-level ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges org-wide so no team's workload can silently consume unbounded shared capacity - node pool segregation is usually more cost-effective and simpler to reason about than one cluster per team.
GitOps drift under pressure: During an i: In a GitOps setup such as ArgoCD or Flux, the controller continuously reconciles the live cluster state back to match what is declared in Git - a manual kubectl edit is exactly the kind of drift the controller is designed to detect and revert, so the hotfix gets silently overwritten on the next sync. The correct emergency path is to make the same change in the Git-tracked manifest/Helm values and let the controller apply it, using an expedited/manual sync if the pipeline supports one, or if speed is critical, temporarily pause auto-sync for that specific application, apply the manual fix, and immediately follow up with a Git commit reflecting the change before re-enabling auto-sync. Never leave a manual change unsynced with Git, since it will eventually be silently reverted or confuse the next person.
Cross-region latency regression: After a: Suspect shared-resource contention introduced indirectly by the new service - check whether it is colocated on the same nodes/node pool as the affected service and competing for CPU/network bandwidth, whether it is hitting the same shared dependency such as a database, cache, or internal API and adding enough load to slow that dependency for everyone, or whether it changed shared infrastructure config such as a new ingress rule, a service mesh policy, or a network policy that adds overhead to unrelated traffic. Use distributed tracing if available to see where the extra latency actually accumulates in the request path, and check node-level resource graphs (CPU steal, network saturation) for the time window latency regressed - the fix is almost always isolating the new service with a dedicated node pool, connection pool, or rate limit rather than anything in the affected endpoint's own code.
